title: The name of Jesus, not spells
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτα οὐκ οἶδα πόθεν κινούμενος ὁ Κέλσος φησὶ δαιμόνων τινῶν ὀνόμασι καὶ κατακηλήσεσι δοκεῖν ἰσχύειν Χριστιανοὺς, ὡς οἶμαι αἰνισσόμενος τὰ περὶ τῶν κατεπᾳδόντων τοὺς δαίμονας καὶ ἐξελαυνόντων. ἔοικε δὲ σαφῶς συκοφαντεῖν τὸν λόγον. οὐ γὰρ κατακηλήσεσιν ἰσχύειν δοκοῦσιν ἀλλὰ τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ μετὰ τῆς ἀπαγγελίας τῶν περὶ αὐτὸν ἱστοριῶν. ταῦτα γὰρ λεγόμενα πολλάκις τοὺς δαίμονας πεποίηκεν ἀνθρώπων χωρισθῆναι. καὶ μάλισθ᾿ ὅταν οἱ λέγοντες ἀπὸ διαθέσεως ὑγιοῦς καὶ πεπιστευκυίας γνησίως αὐτὰ λέγωσι, τοσοῦτον μέν γε δύναται τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Ἰησοῦ κατὰ τῶν δαιμόνων, ὡς ἔσθ᾿ ὅτε καὶ ὑπὸ φαύλων ὀνομαζόμενον ἀνύειν· ὅπερ διδάσκων ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔλεγε τό· „πολλοὶ ἐροῦσί μοι ἐν ἐκείνῃ τῇ ἡμέρᾳ· τῷ ὀνόματί σου δαιμόνια ἐξεβάλομεν καὶ δυνάμεις ἐποιήσαμεν.“ τοῦτο δ᾿ οὐκ οἶδα πότερον ἑκὼν παρεῖδε καὶ κακουργεῖ ὁ Κέλσος ἢ μὴ ἐπιστάμενος. κατηγορεῖ δ᾿ ἐν τοῖς ἑξῆς καὶ τοῦ σωτῆρος, ὡς γοητείᾳ δυνηθέντος ἃ ἔδοξε παράδοξα πεποιηκέναι καὶ προϊδόντος ὅτι μέλλουσι καὶ ἄλλοι τὰ αὐτὰ μαθήματα ἐγνωκότες ποιεῖν τὸ αὐτὸ, σεμνυνόμενοι τῷ θεοῦ δυνάμει ποιεῖν· οὕστινας ἀπελαύνει τῆς ἑαυτοῦ πολιτείας ὁ Ἰησοῦς. καὶ κατηγορεῖ αὐτοῦ ὅτι, εἰ δικαίως ἀπελαύνει καὶ αὐτὸς ἔνοχος ὢν τοῖς αὐτοῖς, φαῦλός ἐστιν· εἰ δ᾿ αὐτὸς οὐ φαῦλος ταῦτα ποιήσας, οὐδ᾿ οἱ ὁμοίως αὐτῷ πράττοντες. ἄντικρυς δὲ, κἂν δοκῇ ἀνέλεγκτον εἶναι τὸ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ, πῶς ταῦτα ἐποίησε, σαφὲς ὅτι Χριστιανοὶ οὐδεμιᾷ μελέτῃ ἐπῳδῶν χρώμενοι τυγχάνουσιν ἀλλὰ τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Ἰησοῦ καὶ ἄλλων λόγων πεπιστευμένων κατὰ τὴν θείαν γραφήν.
pass_a_gloss: After these things, I do not know from where moved (κινέω), Celsus says that Christians seem (δοκέω) to have strength (ἰσχύω) by names (ὀνόματα) of certain demons/daemons (δαίμονες) and incantations/charmings (κατακήλησις), as I think hinting (αἰνίσσομαι) at matters about those who charm away (κατεπᾴδω) demons and drive them out (ἐξελαύνω). He seems clearly to slander (συκοφαντέω) the teaching. For not by incantations do they seem to be strong but by the name of Jesus with the recital (ἀπαγγελία) of the stories (ἱστορίαι) about him. For these, being spoken, have often made demons be separated (χωρίζω) from men. And especially when those speaking say them from a sound (ὑγιής) and genuinely (γνησίως) having-believed (πιστεύω) disposition (διάθεσις). So much indeed can (δύναμαι) the name of Jesus against demons, that sometimes even named by worthless men (φαῦλοι) it accomplishes (ἀνύω); which teaching, Jesus said: 'many will say to me on that day: in your name we cast out (ἐκβάλλω) demons and did powers/miracles (δυνάμεις).' This I do not know whether Celsus willingly (ἑκών) overlooked (παροράω) and acts maliciously (κακουργέω), or not knowing (ἐπίσταμαι). He accuses in what follows the Savior too, as by sorcery (γοητεία) having been able to do the things he seemed to have done that were paradoxical (παράδοξα), and having foreseen (προοράω) that others too, having known the same lessons (μαθήματα), will do the same, priding themselves (σεμνύνομαι) on doing by God's power; whom Jesus drives out (ἀπελαύνω) of his own commonwealth (πολιτεία). And he accuses him that, if he justly drives them out, being himself liable (ἔνοχος) to the same things, he is worthless (φαῦλος); but if he himself is not worthless having done these things, neither are those acting like him. Directly (ἄντικρυς), even if the matter about Jesus, how he did these things, seems untestable/irrefutable (ἀνέλεγκτος), it is clear that Christians succeed using no practice (μελέτη) of spells (ἐπῳδαί) but the name of Jesus and other words believed according to the divine Scripture (θεία γραφή).
pass_b_english: After this Celsus says (what moves him to it I do not know) that Christians appear to gain their power by the names of certain demons and by incantations. He is hinting, I suppose, at those who cast spells on demons and drive them out. But he seems plainly to be slandering our teaching. For Christians do not appear to gain their power by incantations, but by the name of Jesus, together with the telling of the stories about him. These words, when spoken, have often made demons depart from men, especially when those who say them speak from a sound disposition of genuine faith.

Indeed, the name of Jesus has such power against demons that it is sometimes effective even when named by bad men. Jesus taught this when he said: “Many will say to me on that day, ‘In your name we cast out demons and did mighty works’” (Matthew 7:22). Whether Celsus passed over this on purpose and with malice, or from ignorance, I do not know.

In what follows he also accuses the Savior, saying that it was by sorcery that he was able to do the marvels he appeared to have done; and that he foresaw that others too, having learned the same lessons, would do the same thing and would boast that they did it by the power of God; and that Jesus drives such men out of his own commonwealth. And he accuses him thus: if he drives them out justly, while he himself is liable to the same charges, he is a bad man; but if he is not a bad man for having done these things, neither are those who act as he did.

But to speak plainly: even if it seems impossible to put to the test how Jesus did these things, it is clear that Christians use no practice of spells, but the name of Jesus and other words believed in accordance with the divine Scripture.

choices.choice: Matthew 7:22 is quoted in shortened form: Origen omits 'Lord, Lord' and 'did we not prophesy in your name', and turns the questions into statements; the translation follows Origen's wording. Celsus's charges are reported indirectly (δοκεῖν, ὡς, ὅτι), so they stay outside quotation marks. Celsus's picture of Jesus foreseeing imitators who claim God's power likely reflects Matthew 24:24 (false christs and false prophets with great signs) and Matthew 7:23 ('depart from me'); possible allusions, not cited inline since the words are Celsus's paraphrase. δαίμονες rendered 'demons' throughout, as Origen understands them. ἀνέλεγκτον taken as 'beyond testing' (it cannot be checked how Jesus did his works); 'irrefutable' is the other possible sense, with the same force for the argument. 'ἃ ἔδοξε παράδοξα πεποιηκέναι' rendered 'the marvels he appeared to have done'. In the last sentence τυγχάνουσιν with χρώμενοι is the idiom 'in fact use', and τῷ ὀνόματι is a second object of χρώμενοι; the genitive ἄλλων λόγων is loosely joined and rendered 'other words'.

Wrong sense fixed in the last sentence: 'make no use of spells, but succeed by the name of Jesus' to 'use no practice of spells, but the name of Jesus and other words' (τυγχάνω + participle is not 'succeed'; the name is the object of χρώμενοι)
'moved by what I do not know' to a natural parenthesis '(what moves him to it I do not know)' (οὐκ οἶδα πόθεν κινούμενος)
'from a sound disposition that has truly believed' to 'from a sound disposition of genuine faith' (removed stiff Greek-order calque)
Added nested single quotes for the speech inside Matthew 7:22
